article.body:
chayolim just like you. Welcome to our podcast, where

Chayolim, in what way can this week’s lesson make a difference to you? What changes can you make in your own life?

But … don’t let it stop here! Conduct your own interviews at the Shabbos table. Choose someone

to be the podcast’s guest, and together explore how to live with the messages from the parsha.

Note: These images are for illustrative purposes only and are not meant to be an accurate depiction of the holy faces of the Tzaddikim.

Today in school, we went on an end-of- the-year trip to an amusement park. I really, really wanted to buy a refreshing ice-cold drink, but I had no money on me!

Yeah, it was! But then I was standing in line for a ride, and there was a kid who didn't look Jewish standing in front of me. He dropped a ten- dollar bill without realizing it.

Oh man, ten whole dollars? That could make you rich!

Definitely. I picked it up and thought, “Hey, I could use this to buy soda for myself and my friend!”

Well, that's obvious! I tapped the boy on his shoulder and gave it back to him.

Actually, he was kind of shocked that I didn't just keep it for myself. I told him that G-d is always watching what we do— it’s in one of the 12 Pesukim, after all: “וְהִּנֵה ה' נִצָב עָלָיו״—and of course, the right thing is to return money to its rightful owner!

He was a nasi of the Sanhedrin, and he's quoted in Pirkei Avos. Let’s go for it!

Hello, Rabi Shimon. We were just talking about making a Kiddush Hashem. Do you have any stories about that?

Of course! Let me tell you about the time I spent a whole day running around the market!

Well, it's a bit of a story. You see, I was a very poor man. To earn a parnassa, I gathered chestnuts, turned them into ink, and sold it that way. For a while, I was doing all the shlepping by foot, which wastes a lot of time that could be used for limmud Torah.

Well, one day, I sold some of my belongings and bought a mule from the market to help me carry everything. When I got home, my students found a pouch around its neck—with a very expensive diamond inside!

What a wonderful Hashgacha Pratis! That means you wouldn’t be poor anymore!

Ah! That's what my students thought, as well. But chas v’shalom! I paid the Yishma’eli merchant for the mule, not for the diamond! I quickly ran back and returned it to him.

Hashem commands us to do so in Parshas Emor: “ְוְֹלא ְתְַחְַלְלּו ֶאֶת ֵׁשׁם ָקְָדְִׁשׁי ְוְִנְִקְַדְַׁׁשִּׁתּי ְּבְתֹוְך ְּבְֵנֵי ִיְִׂשָׂרֵָאֵל—do not desecrate My holy name, and I will become kadosh (holy) among the Yidden.”

That's what happened to our brother Chaim today! When he returned the lost money, the owner was so impressed.

Yeah. He said, “Wow! I didn't realize you Jews were such good people. Your religion must be something special.”

That's exactly what happens when we make a kiddush Hashem! We show the world how wonderful Yiddishkeit is.

Aww, now I wish someone would drop money in front of me, too!

Bochur, defeating the Yetzer Hara also brings honor to Hashem’s name.
